podcast.title: Production by Josh Homme (2009)
podcast.body: Josh Homme took on the role of producer for the Arctic Monkeys' `Humbug` album in 2009, recording it at his personal studio, Pink Duck. "a band for which he produced the Humbug album in 2009 at his own studio."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Secrets of Queens of the Stone Age: Part 2

podcast.title: Alex Turner's Dominance in Latest Album
podcast.body: The recent work gives the strong impression that Alex Turner is predominating, and the album sounds more like a great musician (Turner) with a backing band rather than a solid, united group. This perception stems from the fact that Turner practically composed and recorded the album in solitary, and for the first time, he is credited as a producer without the involvement of other band members. "La sensación de que tenemos unos artimon que dicen los que tenemos a un líder al externer que está predominando, sobre todo. Y en el fondo nos está pasando el disco que no suena a un gran músico que le sea al externer con una banda de apoyo que podía ser el resto de artimon que es un líder."

srcs.source: Music Radar Clan
srcs.episode: ARCTIC MONKEYS - Tranquility Base Hotel & Casino. Por qué tiene más sentido del que parece

podcast.title: Alex Turner's Lyrical Talent
podcast.body: Alex Turner is recognized as one of the best lyricists of his generation in non-hip hop music, possibly one of the best alt-rock lyricists since Morrissey. He developed a habit of writing song lyrics in the back of his school books when bored in high school.

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Band's Initial Unawareness of Online Sharing
podcast.body: Initially, the Arctic Monkeys were unaware that their music was being posted online. They only began to notice the impact when crowds at their gigs grew larger and a significant number of fans were singing along to songs the band hadn't officially released.

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Blurring Line of Retro Reinterpretation
podcast.body: The new album navigates a very fine line between retro reinterpretation and directly adopting a non-reinterpreted retro sound. The band heavily relies on classic sounds from Gainsbourg and retro-futurism reminiscent of Kubrick films, but often lacks a reinterpretation vision. This places the album on the edge of sounding like "elevator music" rather than a fresh take on the past. "Es una línea muy fina en la que al estar en la banda se basa muchísimo en esos sonidos clásicos de Gamesburg y del retro futurismo que a veces recuerda a las películas de Kubrick, pero sin embargo no tiene muchas veces esa visión de reinterpretación, esa inversión reinterpretada."

srcs.source: Music Radar Clan
srcs.episode: ARCTIC MONKEYS - Tranquility Base Hotel & Casino. Por qué tiene más sentido del que parece

podcast.title: Creative Ambition vs. Public Expectation
podcast.body: As artists, the Arctic Monkeys are still young and professionally ambitious, and they are not obligated to create music solely to please a 20-year-old audience, especially as established millionaires. Instead, they should produce works that they creatively consider professionally fulfilling, despite the importance of pleasing their audience. "Un artisan no tiene por qué vivir obsesionado con agradar a su público y es bastante sana exactitud."

srcs.source: Music Radar Clan
srcs.episode: ARCTIC MONKEYS - Tranquility Base Hotel & Casino. Por qué tiene más sentido del que parece

podcast.title: Defying Music Industry Fears
podcast.body: At a time when the music industry was "freaking out" over file sharing, the Arctic Monkeys leveraged it to become famous. Despite industry warnings that giving away music for free would lead to financial ruin, the band continued to embrace online sharing. This approach proved that sharing music online could broaden and deepen a band's appeal, setting a new standard for rapidly building a passionate fanbase.

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Demo Distribution Strategy
podcast.body: Arctic Monkeys adopted a distinctive approach to gaining popularity: instead of selling their home-made CD demos at small concerts, they gave them away for free. They understood that the added value came from people knowing their songs rather than purchasing their material, a strategy that significantly boosted their popularity. "ellos no intentaban vender sus pequeños discos en los conciertos sino que lo regalaban. Sabían que el valor añadido precisamente era que la gente supiese las canciones."

srcs.source: Music Radar Clan
srcs.episode: Arctic Monkeys: Cómo nació un mito.

podcast.title: Domino Records Signing and Debut Single Success
podcast.body: After indie labels began to take notice of their online popularity, the group signed with Domino. Their very first single released through the label debuted at number one on the British singles charts in October 2005. "The Arctic Monkeys, their debut album, whatever people say I am, that's what I'm not, set a record for the fastest-selling debut album in the history of British music."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Early 2000s Indie Rock Revival Context
podcast.body: The Arctic Monkeys emerged as part of the early 2000s rock revival alongside bands like Franz Ferdinand, Interpol, Block Party, and The Strokes. Like many of their contemporaries, the band initially operated within a predictable musical trajectory, solidifying and improving their style without venturing too far from their comfort zone. "Cuando pensamos en la generación en la que salían los Artic Monkeys, todas las bandas estaban un poco en esa situación. Afiró, Franfernan, Interpol, Block Party, los Strokes, todas estas bandas que salían a primeros del 2000, en este rival del Rock, el que formaban parte de los Artic Monkeys."

srcs.source: Music Radar Clan
srcs.episode: ARCTIC MONKEYS - Tranquility Base Hotel & Casino. Por qué tiene más sentido del que parece

podcast.title: Early Lyrical Prowess
podcast.body: The Arctic Monkeys' songs are constructed in a very distinctive fashion, and their lyrics are considered "above and beyond so many bands." The band achieved fame while still teenagers.

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Embracing File Sharing for Fame
podcast.body: The Arctic Monkeys are sometimes credited as the first band to effectively use the internet to break through to a mass audience, achieving this when they were in their late teens and early twenties. In 2003, they began recording demos at Sheffield's Two Fly studio, accumulating 22 tracks by the following year. These demos were burned onto CDs and given away at gigs for two years, leading fans to rip them to MP3s and share them online.

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Evolution vs. Radical Change Dilemma
podcast.body: The band's drastic stylistic change is seen by some as a "professional suicide" if viewed solely through the lens of their previous albums. However, if one considers their side projects, such as The Last Shadow Puppets' recent album, the shift appears as a "not predictable but quite logical" evolution, indicating a broader vision for the band's trajectory. "Si nosotros consideramos que los álbumes del ASEADO PAPETS es parte de la escorrafía de Artic Monkeys, este álbum es un salto menos al vacío de lo que pueda aparecer."

srcs.source: Music Radar Clan
srcs.episode: ARCTIC MONKEYS - Tranquility Base Hotel & Casino. Por qué tiene más sentido del que parece

podcast.title: Fan Disappointment and "Selling Out" Accusations
podcast.body: Many fans felt disappointed by the band's decision to sign with a record label, perceiving it as "selling out" or becoming too involved with the mainstream music industry. They were criticized for attending awards ceremonies like the Brit Awards and participating in the "fanfare" of the music industry. "mucha gente que los ha atachado de vendidos o que han acabado llendo a recoger premios, actuando los brita wards un poco metidos en todo ese fan anduleo de la industria discográfica."

srcs.source: Music Radar Clan
srcs.episode: Arctic Monkeys: Cómo nació un mito.

podcast.title: Fan-Driven Internet Popularity
podcast.body: The band's audience played a crucial role in their rise to fame by actively sharing the physical copies of the demos they received at concerts. Fans would upload these recordings to the internet, and file sharing greatly contributed to their widespread recognition. "era su público el que compartía en mano esas copias de sus pequeños discos que regalaban en los conciertos, los subía internet, el intercambio de archivos los ayudó en Monton."

srcs.source: Music Radar Clan
srcs.episode: Arctic Monkeys: Cómo nació un mito.

podcast.title: Future Discussion Topic
podcast.body: The Arctic Monkeys are mentioned as a pending topic for future discussion, indicating their relevance within contemporary music analysis. "por un lado es Arctic Monkage... que lo habéis pedido muchas veces y se ha ido demorando."

srcs.source: Music Radar Clan

podcast.title: High Green Isolation
podcast.body: All four members of the band originated from High Green, an isolated northern suburb of Sheffield. During their formative years, the lack of a direct transit connection to downtown meant young residents often stayed within their neighborhood, fostering local activities like forming bands. This close proximity, with everyone living within a ten-minute walk and attending the same school, facilitated the band's formation.

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Industry Disruption with MySpace
podcast.body: The band's innovative use of MySpace to build a massive online following before signing a record deal fundamentally challenged traditional music industry practices. Their success with a debut album whose songs were already freely available online demonstrated a new path for artists to launch careers and reach audiences directly. "The Arctic Monkeys basically broke the music industry with their use of MySpace."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The 100 Greatest Rock Moments of the Millennium So Far - Part 1: (100-91)

podcast.title: Influence from The Strokes
podcast.body: Arctic Monkeys were among the bands explicitly mentioned as crediting The Strokes as an influence on their music. "Other bands crediting the strokes as an influence include Arctic Monkeys, Franz Ferdinand, and LCD Sound System."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Intermediate Path in the Music Industry
podcast.body: Arctic Monkeys are seen as a band stuck on an intermediate path, balancing complete independence from the industry with the necessity of relying on it for their work. This position led to disappointment among hardcore fans who expected total independence, while the industry perhaps anticipated greater compliance. "se han quedado en ese camino intermedio, que a veces es difícil de situar y difícil definir."

srcs.source: Music Radar Clan
srcs.episode: Arctic Monkeys: Cómo nació un mito.

podcast.title: Internet-Savvy Origins in Sheffield
podcast.body: A very young, erudite, and internet-conscious band from Sheffield, the Arctic Monkeys gained early traction by giving away their music at gigs and embracing fans sharing their songs for free on MySpace. "The Arctic Monkeys started by giving away their music at gigs and didn't care when fans put their songs up for free on MySpace."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Joshua Tree Studio Client
podcast.body: The Arctic Monkeys are noted as having been clients of the studio in Joshua Tree, California. This studio, which also functions as the owner's residence, hosted the Foo Fighters for the recording of "Outside." "Arctic monkeys,"

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Legendary Albums at Olympic
podcast.body: The Arctic Monkeys, among a host of other artists, recorded legendary albums at Olympic Studios. "Oasis, U2, the Arctic Monkeys, the Killers, the Pesh Mode, Moracy, Pink Floyd, Massive Attack, the Spice Girls, Adele and dozens and dozens of others made legendary albums at Olympic."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Live Performance on Jimmy Fallon
podcast.body: During their first performance of the new material on Jimmy Fallon, the band of tracks appeared more like an accompanying orchestra or a backing band, similar to those David Bowie had, rather than the solid band sound that the Arctic Monkeys had always projected. This reinforced the idea of Alex Turner's dominant role. "Y ahora la primera actuación que hacía en los artichmon que hice este nuevo trabajo en el show de Jimmy Fallon y lo veíamos muy claro. Y una banda de tracks que parecía más una orquesta de acompañamiento parecía más una banda de acompañamiento como las que tuvo David Bowie y no tanto una banda sólida que es el sonido que siempre ha mientido en los artichmon que hice."

srcs.source: Music Radar Clan
srcs.episode: ARCTIC MONKEYS - Tranquility Base Hotel & Casino. Por qué tiene más sentido del que parece

podcast.title: Logo Inspiration
podcast.body: The inspiration for the Arctic Monkeys' logo is observed to be similar to other characteristic genre logos. "Ahora que me fijó ya sé de dónde ha sacado la inspiración para su logo Artic Monkeys."

srcs.source: Central Sonora
srcs.episode: Cómo los Logos Definieron la Música ｜ Símbolos de Resistencia

podcast.title: Loss of Band Essence in New Album
podcast.body: While the band has evolved and taken a leap, they have lost a part of their essence, which is regrettable as many artists who reinvent themselves manage to retain their core DNA. Unlike Beck or Radiohead's Kid A, where a pure essence was maintained, the Arctic Monkeys failed to keep a thread of their unique identity in their latest work. "Es una pena que los artidmonks hayan hecho este salto al vacío sin saber mantener una parte de su ADN que es interesante para mantener un hilo conductor en la discuracia de la banda."

srcs.source: Music Radar Clan
srcs.episode: ARCTIC MONKEYS - Tranquility Base Hotel & Casino. Por qué tiene más sentido del que parece

podcast.title: Matt Helders' Drummer Origin
podcast.body: Matt Helders became the band's drummer by necessity, as all other instruments were already claimed, making him the "Ringo" of the group. His background included being "very much into beats" and listening to Motown due to his parents' influence. By his teens, he was deeply immersed in hip hop, with Wu Tang, Outcast, and Eminem as favorites, and he harbored dreams of becoming a DJ by age 14.

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Matt Helders' Hip Hop and Dance Scene Disillusionment
podcast.body: By the late 1990s, Matt Helders' interest in the dance scene, encompassing genres like garage and jungle, waned as it became more commercial ("big money territory"). This shift was a "huge turnoff" for those who preferred the underground nature of these scenes.

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Media Frenzy for Internet Breakthrough
podcast.body: When the media recognized that the Arctic Monkeys were poised to be the first band to achieve mainstream success through the internet, a "frenzy" ensued, intensifying their rapid rise to fame.

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: MySpace Discovery
podcast.body: The band gained attention from numerous record labels after fans began posting their early do-it-yourself recordings on MySpace. This illustrates a shift in how A&R departments scouted new talent, leveraging online platforms. "They came to the attention of a lot of record labels as the result of fans posting their early do-it-yourself recordings to my space."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: MySpace Fan-Driven Success
podcast.body: Despite the band not knowing what MySpace was, their fanbase grew exponentially because fans created tribute pages on the platform featuring their music. "The Arctic Monkeys had no idea what MySpace was, but they benefited from fans who created tribute pages with their music."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: MySpace Strategy and Viral Success
podcast.body: Arctic Monkeys were an early adopter of MySpace, choosing to upload all their music onto the platform for free listening and encouraging fans to share it widely. This unconventional strategy proved highly effective, leading the band to go viral on MySpace, sell out gigs rapidly, and generate significant buzz that attracted record labels. "Against all conventional wisdom, they started uploading all their music onto MySpace."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The 100 Greatest Rock Moments of the Millennium So Far - Part 1: (100-91)

podcast.title: New Wave of Alt-Rock
podcast.body: The Arctic Monkeys were part of a new crop of indie artists who emerged after the alt-rock bottomed out, many of whom operated outside the standard music industry model, signaling a return for alt-rock in a few years. "They had names like The Arctic Monkeys, Arcade Fire, The White Stripes, The Killers, and The Strokes."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Nick Lowe Influence
podcast.body: Alex Turner, the songwriter for the Arctic Monkeys, considers Nick Lowe to be one of his all-time favorite songwriters. This acknowledges Lowe's enduring influence on contemporary artists and his significant contributions to songwriting beyond the Powerpop genre. "If you ask Alex Turner of the Arctic Monkeys who his favorite songwriter of all time is, he will tell you that one of them has got to be Nick Lowe."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Origin Story - Bored Sheffield Students
podcast.body: The band's story began with four young students from Sheffield who, out of boredom and being poor students, started playing music because there was nothing more interesting to do. They quickly rose to fame through the internet and became a significant reference point in the music industry. "cuatro chavales de Sheffield, que se aburrían en amalos estudiantes, tocaban porque no tenían otra cosa más interesante que hacer y un buen día interno se hace famosos y se convierten en un referente de la industria de la música."

srcs.source: Music Radar Clan
srcs.episode: Arctic Monkeys: Cómo nació un mito.

podcast.title: Pioneers of the Indie Rock Revival (Early 2000s)
podcast.body: The Arctic Monkeys were among the "new, sharp clever bands" that emerged during the Indie Rock Revival or Post-Punk Revival period around 2000-2001. This movement was a refurbished version of old-school early alt-rock, garage rock, and punk styles. "We gave us new, sharp clever bands like the strokes and the hives, the yay-yaz, friends ferdinand, interpool, and the arctic monkeys."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The 100 Greatest Rock Moments of the Millennium So Far - Part 2: (90-81)

podcast.title: Pioneers of the Indie Rock Revival (Early 2000s)
podcast.body: The Arctic Monkeys emerged as part of the early 2000s rock revival alongside bands like Franz Ferdinand, Interpol, Block Party, and The Strokes. podcast.title: Produced by James Ford
podcast.body: James Ford, who also produced Depeche Mode's *Spirit* album, is known for his work as a producer for the Arctic Monkeys. "es también productor de gente como los Artic Monkeys."

srcs.source: Music Radar Clan

podcast.title: Right Music, Right Time
podcast.body: A significant factor in Arctic Monkeys' success was their ability to produce the appropriate music at the opportune moment. They offered a style that was experiencing rapidly increasing demand but had limited supply within the rising Rock Revival movement. "hacían la música adecuada en el momento adecuado."

srcs.source: Music Radar Clan
srcs.episode: Arctic Monkeys: Cómo nació un mito.

podcast.title: Sheffield Origins
podcast.body: The Arctic Monkeys hail from Sheffield, England, a city with a rich musical history, particularly noted for synth pop in the 1980s and the subsequent era of Acid House. Growing up in Sheffield in the 90s meant being aware of its diverse music scene.

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Signing with Domino Records - Creative Freedom Clause
podcast.body: Arctic Monkeys eventually signed with Domino Records, a label also associated with Franz Ferdinand and significant in the classic rock revival. Despite fan disappointment, this move was inevitable for releasing material in 2005-2006. Notably, their contract included a clause guaranteeing extreme creative freedom, even allowing them the liberty to never record an album, a detail literally written into the agreement. "afirmaron en el contrato que tenían que ser tan libres que podían ser hasta ser libres de no llegar nunca a grabar ningún disco. Y esto físicamente lo llegaron a grabar en el contrato."

srcs.source: Music Radar Clan
srcs.episode: Arctic Monkeys: Cómo nació un mito.

podcast.title: The Sheriff's Crucial Role
podcast.body: A fan named Mark Bull, known as "The Sheriff" in Arctic Monkeys lore, was instrumental in their online breakthrough. He is believed to be the first person to post the band's demo tracks online for public access. As the band distributed more songs and played more shows, The Sheriff continued to upload their material, collecting it under the title "Beneath the Boardwalk," a reference to one of the band's regular venues. His website eventually hosted 18 Arctic Monkeys songs.

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: UK Alt Rock Success (2010s)
podcast.body: This band was noted for its strong chart performance in the UK alt-rock scene during the 2010s, emerging from indie labels. "Arctic Monkeys, Mumford & Sons, Fools, Alt J, Toot or Cinema Club."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The History of the 2010s Part 2: The Role of Indie Rock

podcast.title: Unbeknownst MySpace Profile
podcast.body: MySpace was instrumental in popularizing Arctic Monkeys, but intriguingly, the band's official MySpace profile was not created by them. Two fans from Sheffield, who were deeply fond of the band, set up the page without the band's knowledge. This detail was later verified as completely true. "el Mayespace Social de los Artigmonkeys no era de los Artigmonkeys. Era de dos chavales también de Sheffield que eran muy fans de la banda y que hicieron el Mayespace de ellos. Pero ellos no sabían ni que tenían un Mayespace."

srcs.source: Music Radar Clan
srcs.episode: Arctic Monkeys: Cómo nació un mito.

podcast.title: Unusual Path to Fame
podcast.body: The way the Arctic Monkeys became famous was completely antithetical to the conventional methods of the music business. Their approach to gaining an audience made them unusual but earned admiration.

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Virtuous Circle of Internet Growth
podcast.body: The online sharing of demos, facilitated by The Sheriff, created a "virtuous circle" of increasing popularity. Fans downloaded, shared, burned, and created MySpace sites dedicated to the songs. This led to widespread word-of-mouth, more downloads, and larger attendance at gigs, establishing a self-generating community that grew rapidly.

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Worst Offenders in Loudness Wars
podcast.body: The Arctic Monkeys are specifically named as one of the "worst offenders" among bands whose recent albums suffer from excessive compression, leading to an unrelenting loudness that causes listener fatigue. "The worst offenders that I found are the Arctic monkeys, the chili peppers, the killers, mues, queens of the Stone Age, and of course Metallica."

xref.title: Breakup in 2011
xref.body: The White Stripes officially announced their breakup on February 2, 2011, stating it was for "a myriad of reasons, mostly to preserve what is beautiful and special about the band." The band had an influential run from 1997 through 2011, becoming a major part of the Indy Rock revival of the early 2000s alongside bands like The Strokes and Arctic Monkeys. The reasons for the split included Meg White's introverted nature and desire for a personal life, the end of her marriage to Jack White, and Jack's diverging musical ambitions. Following the breakup, Meg White receded into obscurity, while Jack White continued as a solo performer and music industry figure. "The official breakup announcement came on February 2, 2011."

These demos were burned onto CDs and given away at gigs for two years, leading fans to rip them to MP3s and share them online.

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Industry Disruption with MySpace
xref.body: The band's innovative use of MySpace to build a massive online following before signing a record deal fundamentally challenged traditional music industry practices. Their success with a debut album whose songs were already freely available online demonstrated a new path for artists to launch careers and reach audiences directly. "The Arctic Monkeys basically broke the music industry with their use of MySpace."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.body: Matt Helders, the drummer for Arctic Monkeys, formed "new allegiances" to The Strokes as he gravitated towards guitar-based indie bands.

xref.title: Influence on Matt Helders' Drumming
xref.body: The D4, specifically the style of their drummer Daniel Pooley, combined with Matt Helders' early exposure to dance and hip hop, is cited as an explanation for Matt Helders' distinctive drumming style in the Arctic Monkeys.

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Influence on Other Bands
xref.body: The Strokes, particularly with their debut album "Is This It," profoundly influenced many bands that followed, making them one of the most important bands of the 2000s. Kings of Leon learned to play by emulating "Is This It." The Killers, after hearing the album, reportedly scrapped all their existing material except for "Mr. Brightside" and restarted, with elements of The Strokes' construction and recording audible in their music. Other bands like Arctic Monkeys, Franz Ferdinand, and LCD Sound System also credit The Strokes as an influence. "If it wasn't for the Strokes, it's possible that the Indy Rock Garage Rock Revival that took hold in New York City in the early 2000s wouldn't have grown the way it did."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Internet-Savvy Origins in Sheffield
xref.body: A very young, erudite, and internet-conscious band from Sheffield, the Arctic Monkeys gained early traction by giving away their music at gigs and embracing fans sharing their songs for free on MySpace. "The Arctic Monkeys started by giving away their music at gigs and didn't care when fans put their songs up for free on MySpace."

xref.body: When the media recognized that the Arctic Monkeys were poised to be the first band to achieve mainstream success through the internet, a "frenzy" ensued, intensifying their rapid rise to fame.

xref.title: MySpace Fan-Driven Success
xref.body: Despite the band not knowing what MySpace was, their fanbase grew exponentially because fans created tribute pages on the platform featuring their music. "The Arctic Monkeys had no idea what MySpace was, but they benefited from fans who created tribute pages with their music."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

"They had names like The Arctic Monkeys, Arcade Fire, The White Stripes, The Killers, and The Strokes."

xref.title: Nick Lowe Influence
xref.body: Alex Turner, the songwriter for the Arctic Monkeys, considers Nick Lowe to be one of his all-time favorite songwriters. This acknowledges Lowe's enduring influence on contemporary artists and his significant contributions to songwriting beyond the Powerpop genre. "If you ask Alex Turner of the Arctic Monkeys who his favorite songwriter of all time is, he will tell you that one of them has got to be Nick Lowe."

xref.title: Sheffield Origins
xref.body: The Arctic Monkeys hail from Sheffield, England, a city with a rich musical history, particularly noted for synth pop in the 1980s and the subsequent era of Acid House. Growing up in Sheffield in the 90s meant being aware of its diverse music scene.

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.body: The Long Pigs were a Sheffield guitar band that became a favorite of the Arctic Monkeys, serving as a "big influence" on their sound.

xref.title: Songwriting Influence
xref.body: Nick Lowe is a highly influential songwriter, not only having hit singles of his own but also seeing several of his tracks become hits for other artists, including Elvis Costello and Johnny Cash. His talent is recognized by contemporary musicians, with Alex Turner of the Arctic Monkeys citing him as a favorite songwriter. "If you ask Alex Turner of the Arctic Monkeys who his favorite songwriter of all time is, he will tell you that one of them has got to be Nick Lowe."
